utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Groome: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, when we concluded your testimony a week ago, you were describing a meeting you attended with two people by the name of Grujic and Jovo Mijatovic. I'm going to ask you a few more detailed questions about that meeting, but before I do, could you briefly describe, in a sentence or two, who was Brano Grujic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brano Grujic is a citizen of Zvornik of Serb ethnicity, the number one man in Zvornik, the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was Jovo Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovo Mijatovic was one of the leading politicians in the municipality, and he was a deputy in the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, are you familiar with a person by the name of Marko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us in a sentence who he was?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He represented himself as the first commander of the army and all the other units situated within the territory of Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have one final question before I ask you to continue your testimony. Was there a Serb Crisis Staff in the Zvornik area? And if so, can you tell us where its headquarters was located?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Crisis Staff for Zvornik municipality based in Zvornik. The president of the staff was Brano Grujic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there a building, a particular building that the Crisis Staff used?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar -- well, let me now draw your attention back to that meeting. At that meeting, were you given an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ultimatum and who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th, in the morning, in Kozluk, in the police station there, Brano Grujic told me that we should immediately move out of Kozluk. He said that when he said "immediately," it meant within an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of that meeting, did anyone indicate to you what would happen if you failed to move out of Kozluk within that period of time?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who advised you what would happen?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovo Mijatovic, a deputy in the National Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, took me to the side and told me that an all-out attack was being prepared on Kozluk, and if we didn't move out that we would all be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after you left that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The reference to "we should move out," who do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only Bosniaks lived in Kozluk. And there were about two to 2.500 Bosniaks left. So the implication was that we Muslims, we Bosniaks, had to move out. That was the order we were given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after you left that meeting?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I asked how could we organise this for 2.500 people, how we could leave Kozluk? Brano Grujic told me not to worry about that at all, that transportation was provided and that we would be deported to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything else of significance that occurred during that meeting before I ask you what you did after you left the meeting?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after you left the meeting?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left quickly, and I sent a number of my associates to get the people together. I took a loudspeaker and called on the people to come. At the very centre of Kozluk there were long columns of military vehicles, tanks, and quite a large number of troops. It was dreadful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where -- was it your intention to assemble the people in a central location?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you attempt to assemble the people of Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the centre of Kozluk, in front of the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the cultural centre, was there anybody that -- there to record the names of the people who were assembling there to leave Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just describe briefly for us the process under which the names of the people were gathered, those people that were leaving Kozluk that day?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of every house there were several soldiers standing, policemen and paramilitary troops. Those men were pushing the people towards the centre. They were opening fire at them. They were beating them. And the people of Kozluk felt like herds of sheep being shepherded into the centre of Kozluk. In the centre of Kozluk, in front of the cultural home, there were about 2.000 people assembled. There were many soldiers, paramilitary units, policemen, and other armed forces. A group of soldiers together with a group of citizens of Kozluk were taking down the names of people. The citizens came up, they signed their names, upon which they entered, they boarded the parked buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, I'd like to show you Prosecution Exhibit tab 4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Prosecution Exhibit 445.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 445, tab 4, a document of several pages. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I note for the Chamber a copy of this will be displayed on the monitors, and for the amici and the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the first page of that document, and I want to draw your attention specifically to the upper right-hand corner. There's a stamp there. I believe it's in blue ink on the original. Can you please read what that stamp says.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Republic -- sorry. The Serbian Municipality of Zvornik, Municipal Staff of Territorial Defence Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the last page of that document and ask you, do you see anywhere on that page your signature?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Chamber what is this document, Prosecution 445, tab 4.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list of the citizens of Kozluk, a list of the heads of households with the number of family members indicated who were moving out of Kozluk in an organised fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a similar document prepared for the people from Skocici?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe where Skocici is in relation to Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skocici is a small locality right next to Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the people from Skocici also required to leave that day?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they, too, assemble in the same place as the people from Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 445, tab 5. And again, is that -- draw your attention to the upper right-hand corner. Is that the same stamp of the Zvornik Territorial Defence in the upper right-hand corner of the first page of that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could I draw your attention once again to the last page and ask you do see your signature on the last page of that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now with respect to tabs 4 and 5, are these both the original documents as you recall from that day?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original documents with the signatures were taken by the members of the Zvornik territorial staff. These are copies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair that those are carbon copies generated on the same day? They're not photocopies made at a later time?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were made on the same day, only the first copy was taken by the people from the Zvornik Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to these documents, did you ever receive a document signed by Major Marko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe the circumstances under which you received that document.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we had assembled in front of the cultural centre and once we had signed the document saying we were leaving Kozluk, then an envelope was opened containing the instructions or order of the commander of the Zvornik Territorial Defence. I saw that document 15 minutes prior to us being expelled from Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 445, tab 6. I'm going to direct your attention to the upper portion, the typewritten portion of that document. Does that document fairly and accurately depict the document as you initially received it on that day?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to read the second paragraph of that document for us.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To the above-mentioned adult persons upon their explicit request, without any duress, having expressed the wish that they wish to avoid at all costs the mobilisation into Muslim formations, a pre-settlement has been approved."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that statement true?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the bottom portion of the document as we have it here in court has some handwritten notes on it. Do you recognise the handwriting on the bottom portion of that document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you make these handwritten notes on top of the document you received?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th, in the afternoon, in Loznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do these notes reflect your calculation about the actual number of people who were forced to leave Kozluk on that day?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give us the number of people you counted that were forced to leave Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five hundred and twenty-five households; 1.822 persons or citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you please describe for the Chamber how the people were physically moved from Kozluk out of Kozluk. What vehicles were used?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the centre of Kozluk, there were 17 buses and three trucks with trailers. There were two passenger vehicles as well. And we travelled in that way from the centre of Kozluk as far as Loznica. From Loznica to Ruma, we continued in those same vehicles, and in Ruma --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you to go step-by-step each portion of the journey. I'd like to ask you a few questions about Loznica. In what republic is Loznica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loznica is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that the first place that the buses stopped after they left Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there border controls on the Serbian side of the border as you crossed into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a border crossing between Bosnia and Serbia at Sepak that is a bridge across the Drina River. That is the border crossing. And this long column of vehicles crossed over to Serbia there and we were stopped there. We were stopped at Loznica next to the Drina river bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in Loznica before you were moved from Loznica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spent about five to six hours there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the Serbian side of the border did you see any persons you recognised as being paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the column of vehicles stopped, a large number of people walked around the convoy and the men. These men wore different uniforms. They were rather dirty, carrying various types of weapons. They were wearing gloves on their hands. They looked awful, like vultures, and they walked around us, demanding that the girls get off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- did you or somebody else make contact with the Serbian police regarding that situation and was there a response by the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were quite frightened. Many of these men were walking around our buses and trucks. They started pulling people by the hand, demanding money. And then I approached a police patrol, and they just asked me to be quiet and that reinforcements would arrive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did police reinforcements arrive and protect the convoy?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three to four vehicles arrived. Quite a large number of policemen came who were tidy, wearing proper uniforms, and they stood around the convoy and the vehicles so that these others didn't dare approach us any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the time you were in Loznica, were you subjected to any mistreatment whatsoever by the members of the Serbian police force?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know a person by the name of Dr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a Serb doctor based in Loznica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you make contact -- I don't believe I've heard the answer.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you make contact with him while you were in Loznica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he come to meet with you along with a representative of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came, they met with me, and they told me that they would give us aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation with them regarding what would be required or who would have to give permission before you would continue your journey?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked them for some food because there were quite a lot of children. And we also asked them to help us to move on, because the frontline was there close by, and there were quite a number of paramilitary units there. And they responded that they would do everything they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there anything said about having to get permission or authorisation for you to continue on your journey?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people from the Red Cross, from Loznica, said that they would send a letter to Belgrade asking for permission for us to be able to continue on our journey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a second meeting with the representative of the Red Cross during which they informed you that such a letter or such authorisation was received?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the afternoon, they came with a paper, and they said, "You're lucky. You've got permission to be able to move on."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at a document, Prosecution Exhibit 445, tab 7, and my question to you is do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you to read the typing on the upper left-hand corner and continue on to the title of the document.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Republic of Serbia, the Commissariat for Refugees," number, then date 26th of June, 1992, Belgrade. "Staff for the reception and care of refugees." I saw this document on the 26th in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Chamber will have the document to read in full, but just to summarise the contents of the document, does this document authorise -- or did it authorise the people of Kozluk to continue their journey through Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after receiving this document, did the convoy move from Loznica to somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The convoy moved on through Serbia in the direction of Ruma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time of the day, approximately, did the convoy arrive in Ruma?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived at Ruma, what happened?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police that escorted us said that there was a train that we would board and that the train would take us further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you and other members of the Kozluk community in fact board a train?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police left, and we got off the buses and trucks and boarded the train. The train had several carriages, and there were quite a number of those intended for cattle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what, if anything, occurred while the people of Kozluk were boarding these trains?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were boarding the train, we were stoned. A large number of citizens threw stones at us, chairs, shouting, "Turks. Alija's army." And quite a number of people were injured on that occasion because this large crowd of 2.000 people were boarding the carriages for livestock. The stones were raining on us, pieces of wood, and quite a number of people were injured. Some in the head, started bleeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, once the people were loaded onto the train, where did the train go?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The train went -- or, rather, we were told we were going to Subotica. And as we travelled, in several other places, stones were thrown at us, and the glass was broken, so the people didn't dare get up. So we had this stoning on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The train that you boarded and took between Ruma and Subotica, was it an ordinary train -- my question to you is were there other people not from Kozluk on that train, or was it a train specially arranged for the people of Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a special train, a train intended for cattle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Subotica, can you tell us approximately when you arrived in Subotica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I know that the trip took a long time and that we arrived in Subotica during daytime. I know that the people were tired, bloody, quite a number of children were sick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first night in Subotica, where did you and the other people on the train, where did they sleep?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Subotica, we slept on stones in the wagons, in the carriages, in the fields. There were about 2.000 people. The conditions were appalling. They were hungry, ill. They spent several days in terrible conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the people were moved to another location?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, we were visited by members of the Red Cross. Quite a significant number of journalists visited us. They filmed us as if we were animals in a circus. They spent a lot of time filming us. People were given first aid. Some of them had injured heads. They then promised to transport us to Palic, to transfer us to Palic, that some kind of a camp or collection centre for those refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were -- were you and other members -- or the other people from Kozluk transferred to this Palic, this refugee centre?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there guards at this refugee centre Palic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what you learnt about the guards that were guarding people of Kozluk in Palic.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they boasted that they had been in the battlefields in Croatia and Bosnia. They kept saying -- shouting and saying that they had killed quite a lot of Turks. They had a terrible appearance. They had beards. And by the way they looked, you could see that they were combatants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the guards at this camp say anything to the people who were detained there regarding what was required for them to be able to leave that camp?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whoever had money, they would sort that person's papers out through connections. They'd sort out passports for them. They were taken away, taken to the station and then they would go to Hungary. Those who didn't have money remained there. They remained in Palic, in the camp in Palic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were able to make contact with some friends of yours in a factory in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to make certain arrangements with these people to assist you and the other people from Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the management of the Suboticanka factory, which is located in Subotica, and there was a group of Hungarians there who were part of the management. As they cooperated well with the same factory in my place, in Kozluk, they brought juice to us. I asked them to assist us, to help us get passports and photographs because we didn't have any money, and this was simply not a possibility for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they make arrangements for photographers to come to take passport photos, and did they take a collection of money to assist in the purchase of passports?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over several days they brought about five photographers who made photographs for the entire population. They came with the chief of police, and in front of us they handed over to him a cheque as a means of payment for those passports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many Serbian passports were issued to the people of Kozluk during this time period?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over a thousand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 445, tab 8. These are two passports. A copy of the photograph page of one of them will be displayed on the screen before you. I would draw your attention to Saha Hadzic's passport. Can you see it on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a citizen from Kozluk. Her name is Saha Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she one of the people who was forced to leave Kozluk in the way that you've described before the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this a photograph of the passport issued by the Republic of Serbia during this time period?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take a look at the other photograph page of the second passport. And do you recognise the two people -- if you look on the screen before you, it's displayed. Do you recognise the two people here?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they two people from Kozluk that were forcibly removed from Kozluk on the 26th of June?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to draw your attention now to the stamp, the issue stamp in this particular passport. And can you -- can you describe -- or I'd ask you just to read, who was this passport issued by?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipal Assembly of Subotica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to look on the monitor. The page is displayed on the monitor before you.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who issued this passport?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretariat in Subotica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what governmental office?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's the date of issue?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after passports were issued, were people then placed on trains and sent to the Hungarian border?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Groups of citizens, as they received their passports, left for the borders in groups. They got on the trains and headed for Hungary and Austria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The trains from Subotica to Hungary and Austria, were they specially arranged trains or were they regularly scheduled passenger trains?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think that these trains had been organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask now that Prosecution Exhibit 445, tab 9, be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, there's a map being placed to your left. Do you recognise this map? You can look to the left. The original is on the projector to your left. Do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who made the markings on this map?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do -- what does the line that you've drawn on this map indicate?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the route we took. It is this route that was used when we were deported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask -- thank you -- that we start from the bottom. I'd ask you to start at Kozluk, and if you would just trace with the pointer the journey that you and the other members of the Kozluk community took, and please indicate where it was you crossed into Serbia. If you'd do it on the -- to your left, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozluk, which is in Bosnia and Herzegovina, is here. We have the Sepak place on the Drina River, and there is a border crossing there. This is the point at which we crossed into Serbia. And we arrived between Banja Koviljaca and Loznica. We spent a certain period of time there, and then we continued on this route in the direction of Sabac and Ruma. We got on a train in Ruma, and about 2.000 people were transported on that train in livestock carriages, and we were stoned on several occasions. The train went in the direction of Subotica. In Subotica, we were placed in accommodation. We slept near the railway. There were quite a few journalists and quite a large number of people had been injured. And then a group of good Hungarians helped us to go to Palic from Subotica. They were from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of this journey, were you ever free to simply leave the convoy and travel throughout Serbia or go where you pleased? Were you ever free to do that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your mind, or what did you observe that indicated to you that the people of Kozluk weren't simply free to disperse into Serbia and go where they wished?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we weren't allowed to take anything with us. Secondly, while we were being deported, we were escorted by the police. We were beaten. We were starving during the transport. We arrived in Subotica. We were taken to -- it wasn't even a station, it was a place where there were a lot of police. It was some sort of a dead end, and we couldn't move. We didn't have any means. We didn't have any documents. We were hostages of those policies. We were taken to Palic, which was a camp of a closed kind. It had guards. Where could we have gone? Nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness's monitor be placed so that he can see something displayed on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned in your testimony that international journalists were present and took pictures of some of these events. I'm going to ask you to look at some pictures contained in a video on the screen before you, and then I'm going to ask if you recognise the pictures and the people in them. I'd ask that we now play it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the people in these photographs?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the train that was used to deport us from Ruma to Subotica. Just those few carriages. The others were livestock carriages and didn't have any windows. These citizens of Kozluk, Mehic Alija, Jakic Zehrudin, Muhamed Kalabankovic [phoen], Mulajbisevic Sana. A large number of fellow citizens of mine with small children. There were women, people who had been injured, people who had suffered a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Banjanovic, first of all, I would like to ask you about this stay of yours in Serbia. As far as I can understand, people in Serbia helped you. They helped you inasmuch as you were refugees. Am I right or not?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, if it's assistance when you're surrounded and prevented from leaving, if one can call being stoned three or five times assistance, if you can call the fact that 30 people were wounded is a form of assistance, sleeping in carriages and next to carriages called assistance, and if we have to listen to stories about how many people were killed in Bosnia and in Croatia, if we call this assistance, then that's assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems that, in your opinion, Serbia shouldn't have allowed you to pass through its territory. Anything could have happened to you in Bosnia in that case. So it seems that we were wrong to help you.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia shouldn't have sent those paramilitary forces to Kozluk, the forces that maltreated honourable Serbs as well as us Bosniaks. And the forces that deported, that caused the deportation of citizens of Kozluk and other citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, let's not go into what you are now claiming. That is quite contrary to what you have been explaining. All the people that you mentioned and what you have read out from these documents here, although you only read parts of the documents, none of this concerns Serbia. Read it out again. Provide tab number 4 again, the yellow square from which you read out the words "Crisis Staff," et cetera, "Municipality of Zvornik," and so on, and read it out again. Read it all out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, the question is: What does the document say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got the document. We've seen it. Now, what do you want to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for example, it says, "The Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then beneath that it says, "The Serbian Autonomous District, Semberija and Majevica," then beneath that, it says, "In the Serbian municipality of Zvornik," and then it says -- I don't know what else it says because I can't remember any more. So we're talking about a different state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that correct, Mr. Banjanovic? We're not talking about Serbia.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another state called Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the commander was from the Republic of Serbia, a certain Marko Pavlovic. And the paramilitary formation called the Nis paramilitary formations dominated there, the Kovice from Loznica, and there were many other paramilitary formations which were in Zvornik, Kozluk, and other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, you know a witness with whom I'm going to discuss the subject of paramilitary formations but you must be aware of the fact that authorities in Serbia cracked down on paramilitary formations, and as far as volunteer units are concerned, their significance was negligible with -- in comparison to the volunteer units in the Bosnia and Herzegovina army. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as far as I and the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the citizens of Serbia are aware, all the prisoners, all the criminals, you let them go free. You released them from prison and they acted as vultures and contaminated the good relations between the Serbs and the Bosniaks in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My dear Mr. Banjanovic, I think you are very badly informed with regard to this matter. No one released prisoners of any kind from prison. Not in Serbia, either, apart from those who had served their sentence. Someone has provided you with bad information.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who were in Kozluk told me about this from the Zuti unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were people from Serbia in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Loznica, Valjevo, Nis, from Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Banjanovic, it seems that there were people who came from the entire area of Serb to Kozluk; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did come to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clear this matter up because we're not going to have too much time. In tab 6, and we can see your handwriting there too, this document, Mr. Banjanovic, let's try and be objective at least to a certain extent. If we view this from the position of the Serbian authorities, the Serbian organs or those of Yugoslavia, if you like, here it says: "We hereby request the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to allow safe and organised passage of persons on the list to the border zone with Hungary. These persons, adults, have been allowed to move out at their explicit request without constraint." As you say, it's not written in the Serbian version but in the Bosnian version. And then it goes on: "And because of their desires they informed us at all costs to avoid mobilisation into Muslim formations. This request has been granted. They have been allowed to leave for passage for the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and other Western European countries. Heads of families confirm with their signatures that their departure is the result of their own wish and that it has been not been induced by any repressive measures. The families that have decided to move out are aware of the risks to their property which they're leaving in the zone of combat operations and they have been informed that the authorities in Zvornik cannot assume full responsibility for the belongings they leave in their houses and apartments." I have just read out what it says here, although there are certain grammatical errors. And then it says the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it says the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik, it says the staff of Territorial Defence, the Autonomous Region of Semberija and Majevica. So the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is to say of the Republic of Serbia, received a letter in which they were requested to allow you -- to make it possible for you who had signed that list, because you wanted to go to Western Europe, they wanted to allow you and make it possible for you to go there. How did the authorities of Yugoslavia react? They tried to help you. You showed -- you were shown a map here. You went to Loznica immediately because that's at the border. That's the Municipality of Loznica; isn't that correct? Isn't that right, Mr. Banjanovic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: People tried to help you. They came to help you. You say that there were various hooligans, various thugs around you. That's what you said, when you moved -- when you crossed into Serbia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then a police patrol turned up, a regular police patrol. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't that police patrol, didn't they say to you that they would ask for reinforcements? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did reinforcements arrive?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say that they behaved correctly and had a correct appearance, which isn't the case for the other people who were at the border? There was a war in Bosnia. The border was there.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police protected you from them, didn't they? Isn't that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could that mob, how could those people have been in Serbia, a neighbouring state?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could you be there?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were forced to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A war was raging there. There was a conflict. Did you tell the police that you were forced to go there?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are forgetting that there were over 3.000 people, armed people who had forced those people to go to the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't interrupt. Now, allow the witness to finish what he wants to say. Let him finish. Mr. Witness, if you want to reply, you can, and you're not to be interrupted. Now, do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You're forgetting that this was forcible deportation. When these people were taken away, within one hour a number of people had been wounded, about ten houses had been torched, looting had started. There was torture, beatings, attempts at shooting people. We were loaded onto trucks, trailers. That document, that written document, and you say that it is grammatically incorrect, your people made that document out, the people from the Serbian municipality. It was signed by Commander Marko Pavlovic who is from Sombor in Serbia, and this was given us to about 15 minutes before we were put onto the vehicles. This was forcible deportation. It wasn't on a voluntary basis, and we were escorted by several thousand paramilitary troops and police in Serbia on the Drina River in Loznica. Thanks to the local police alone, we were saved from those vultures who had already started selecting young girls and had started snatching necklaces and rings from them and had started attacking us. That's the truth. There is no other truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, you say that I am forgetting all this. I don't forget what I heard from your testimony. I've heard about Kozluk. I heard about the place called Kozluk only now during your testimony. I'd never heard about that place before. I don't know what -- what it would be well-known for. But didn't you yourself say that as soon as you had crossed the Drina you were protected by the regular police force from Republika Srpska? They protected you. I assume that there was violence there, that people behaved in various manners and that this could be described as violence, but weren't you protected by the police of Republika Srpska there, of the Republic of Serbia there?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Kozluk is well-known as a multinational place, and there were Serbs and Bosniaks who lived, they were on good terms for hundreds of years, and it was well-known for this. When we crossed into Serbia, we were attacked by several groups of people wearing various sorts of uniforms, wearing gloves. They were dirty people, they were armed people. This was the first contact we had with Serbia. We were attacked in Loznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, I recognise the fact that having the status of a refugee when travelling or fleeing from a given territory, I recognise the fact that it's not pleasant to have such a status. My question was a quite specific one. There were various people, various individuals who wanted to attack you, but you were protected by the police in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police protected us and escorted us all the time from Loznica, from Ruma, from Subotica, and Palic. They protected us and made sure that we wouldn't go anywhere else. And they made sure that we remained in that convoy of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, there was no convoy of death. Was anyone killed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than 20 people were injured in Ruma. I was personally wounded. Citizens stoned us, beat us with chairs. They called us balijas, and they told us to go to Turkey. After Ruma, we were stoned in one place. The train was stoned. The stone -- the train had been quite damaged. This had been filmed by international journalists in Subotica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Gutman filmed that. You said that windows were broken and so on and you said that you were transported in carriages for livestock.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the first two carriages were for passengers and the others were livestock carriages. I repeated this on two occasions and showed it on the monitor. There were two to three carriages which were passenger carriages and the other ones were carriages for livestock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these photographs taken, the ones that you were shown at the end?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Subotica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't see any windows that were broken. All the windows are intact on those carriages. Did they change the carriages? What happened? Or out of gratitude for the assistance that you were provided with by Serbia, did you decide to taint the reputation of these people as much as you can?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia's reputation can't be tainted. You did that. But the doctors checked the bodies of people and provided first aid to over 30 people in Subotica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who, which doctors provided you with first aid? Who examined you? Who examined the people who had been injured? Out of the 2.000 people, there were 30 who were injured in various incidents.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it then?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were stoned in a place called Ruma. A group of Serbs stoned us Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because they said, "Go to Turkey, Alija's army."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They called you Alija's army?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Subotica, only the Hungarians helped you, the Serbs didn't; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who they were, but the doctors who helped us were good. They provided the children with water. The Red Cross arrived. They provided food. The doctors provided assistance. And I must say that we owe a lot to those people. There are good people in Serbia too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see that for what is commendable, you wish to attribute to Hungarians from Subotica. And of course I don't exclude that possibility, because there are many Hungarians living in Subotica. As for everything that is bad, that you attribute to the Serbs. Let's make that clear.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the Serbs but to you who were leading your men over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Banjanovic. I don't know where you see any negative links between the authorities in Serbia and your treatment, but Mr. Groome asked you whether anyone mistreated you, that is among the Serb policemen, and you said no.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's right, isn't it? Not only did they not mistreat you but they also protected you. And then you go on to say that Dr. Nikolic arrived. You mention Dr. Nikolic. Judging by his surname, I assume that he's a Serb. Is that right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they said that they would give you aid, and they did, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, you said that you asked them to help you to move on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you asked them to help you to go on, to go towards Western Europe, which was your destination, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what deportation are you talking about or of any involvement on the part of anybody of Serbia in this when you asked the Red Cross and this Dr. Nikolic to help you to move on, to make progress along your journey. And then we have in tab 7 here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, wait a moment. Wait a moment. One thing at a time. What is being suggested is that you weren't being deported at all. You were asking to go to Western Europe or somewhere, and the Serbs were helping you. That's what's being suggested. What is your comment as to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, on the 26th in the morning, the town mayor of Zvornik, Brano Grujic, gave us orders that within an hour, we should assemble in the centre of Kozluk and to leave Kozluk immediately. So we didn't leave on our own accord but following orders from the front man, the one man in Zvornik, Brano Grujic. Secondly, we were forced out of our homes. Next to each of our house, there were several soldiers, paramilitary men, policemen who were shepherding the people like herds into the centre of town. And thirdly, in Kozluk itself, unseen torture started. Houses were torched. People were beaten, mistreated. Several men were wounded. This was a scene of horror. In less than an hour, the men were boarded onto trucks with trailers and 17 or 18 buses. More than 2.000 men got in, and under police escort as well as accompanied by troops and paramilitary units, we were taken to the border.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But Mr. May, you will agree that there's no point in hearing the same story for a second time. This is not in answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course not. But, Mr. Milosevic, what he's saying is that they were forced out of their homes, put on -- put on a train and driven across Serbia and then forced out. So he's saying it's all part of the same story. You must allow him to give his evidence about it. Now, you were asked specifically, and you can deal with this, about the role of Dr. Nikolic, and it's suggested to you that he was assisting you. Now, can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were brought to Serbia, and the vehicles were parked in the form of a column in the town of Loznica. A large number of paramilitary troops tried to get the young women off, to mistreat us, and then I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you just concentrate for a moment on the role of Dr. Nikolic. We did hear that evidence. Was he assisting you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I knew Mr. Nikolic, and he did help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nikolic was a doctor in Zvornik, in Bosnia, and we knew him. And then the Red Cross and he arrived, and we asked them to give us food and water. And the Red Cross did bring us water and food for the children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, I will come back to the events in Kozluk. I wish to clear up, first, what happened in Serbia. The authorities in Serbia, the Red Cross of Serbia, the police that protected you in Loznica had to deal with a column of buses and trucks of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to any representatives of the authorities of Serbia except for the police whom you -- who you asked to protect you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Red Cross and the local police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And you asked the local police to protect you and they did. As for the Red Cross, as you said a moment ago, you asked them to assist you and to help you continue your journey; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those documents that were written were written by them. This was no mobilisation. And quite a number things were added artificially. They just told us for us to be able to pass through Serbia, they would have to ask Belgrade and that they would send a letter there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's look at tab 7. On that same day, you get a reply. So the authorities in Serbia -- the column of refugees has crossed into Serbia, the buses and trucks. The staff for refugees in Loznica asks the Commission for Refugees, because in the heading, it says Commission for Refugees, Belgrade, the 26th of June, they are replying on the same day. They're not delaying for a moment. And this document says "Staff for the Reception and Care of Refugees." "We examined the written statements of 1.822 persons in 17 buses, three trucks with trailers and two passenger vehicles from Kozluk, Zvornik Municipality (who state that of their own free will and without pressure, they wish to leave the territory of Yugoslavia and travel to Western European countries) and are now refugees temporarily residing in Loznica..." That is what it says. This is what Belgrade is responding to. And it says that they: "... found that the written statements of the above-mentioned persons, given" -- it's rather illegible because it is a poor copy -- "on their own behalf as well as on behalf of their underage family members and children are valid since they were given voluntarily and expressed their will as to where they want to live, which is one of the fundamental human rights. "In view of the above, we believe that the requests of these persons should be met" - and I'm afraid I can't read it - "enable their probably realisation in the sense of the intentions contained in the statements submitted." This was the response they gave you. So I'm saying -- I'm talking about what happened to you in Serbia, because as you know, I was the president of Serbia, and I am interested in the attitude of the authorities, the Red Cross, the Commission for Refugees, and all other entities in Serbia. So the column arrived, the police protected you, the Red Cross came, you asked them to assist you, they did assist you. You asked the police to protect you, they protected you. You asked them to make it possible for you to move on, they did, and you got as far as Subotica; is that right? And then you say that you slept on stones there. I don't know whether in the whole of Vojvodina there are stone beds. In Vojvodina, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not a question. These are endless speeches, endless speeches by you, all of which we'll be able to hear in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where he found rocks in Vojvodina. Maybe he took some rocks with him from Bosnia..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a question. At last we have a question. Would you like to answer that? Just a moment. Let him answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any answer is superfluous. The mistreatment we suffered in Serbia is forgotten, the heads injured in Ruma --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't let's keep this going. Let's deal with it as quickly as we can. It's said that you were exaggerating when you said they slept on rocks. Now, is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We slept on a side railway track. We were not in the station. We were separated on a dead-end railway track and that is where we spent the night, in those carriages. Many people slept alongside the carriages because there wasn't enough room for 2.000 men. People were hungry and thirsty. And a number of international media companies filmed this Golgotha, this suffering and this mistreatment and injuring of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, the media in Serbia did not conceal as to what was happening to refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, unfortunately, it is certainly not pleasant to be a refugee. You said that some angry people threw stones at you, which is quite possible, but the police protected you, as was its duty to do. You say that some 30 people were injured. I don't believe there were that many, but still, the medical staff assisted you and treated them. Incidents are quite possible. My question to you is: What was the reaction of the authorities, meaning both the police and the medical authorities? Now, let's us move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let us move on. We've heard the evidence. We've heard the points you've made. There's no point going over it over and over again, and we've got the documents. So let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on. When I look at these documents, Mr. May, what else could the authorities of Serbia do, I ask you? I beg your pardon. First of all, they say it's a fundamental human right which they wish to protect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said at one point, and I took note of that -- no, no. I'll ask you that later on. Let us see what happened in Palic. You say that you were taken to a camp in Palic. Do you know that Palic is the most significant resort in that area?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they put you up in their own tourist centre. There was no camp at Palic. They put up the refugees in their favourite tourist centre, the favourite tourist resort in the environs of Subotica. Everyone is listening to this and they know what Palic is. What kind of a camp are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not telling the truth. They didn't take us to any hostel or hotel. They took us to a meadow with tents. And there was a wire around it, and there was a gate there, and there were guards with beards who boasted as to how many people they had killed in Croatia and Bosnia. You can't call that a tourist resort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, are we talking about the 26th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did all these bearded men have time to kill those people in Bosnia and then come back to Palic in Subotica? What are you talking about? Why are you making up these things?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on Zvornik occurred on the 8th of April, and these men boasted that they were there in Zvornik and did what they did. And this was on the 26th and the 29th of June. So it's three months later. And Croatia was even before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, why are you making up these things? Are you saying that in Palic you were kept in a kind of concentration camp?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat: We were kept in a meadow, in tents. There was a wire fence around it, and there were guards wearing beards, frightening people and demanding money from people to get them passports. For us, that was a camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's clear things up, please. Mr. Groome asked you how many Serbian passports you received, and you said at the end you all got these passports, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, do you know that there are no Serbian passports? They don't exist.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is Serbian over there, including Serbian passports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you held in your hand a passport which says the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the Serbo-Croatian language and in a foreign language, probably either French or English. So it's a Yugoslav passport. I didn't pay attention when I was looking through your documents, but you yourself read out the date of issue of that passport, the 29th. So this happened to you on the 26th, you travelled, you arrived there, all this was over by the 29th. Didn't they then help you to give you passports because you wanted to travel abroad? You wanted to go to Hungary. Wasn't this a kind of assistance to make it possible for you to get travel documents with which you could travel unhindered abroad like free citizens?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are distorting things. It wasn't three days. The passports were issued over a period of about ten days. They were issued in groups, depending on how much money people had. The more people paid -- this was public crime committed by those people in Palic. The guards, the people who had money paid plenty for it, got a passport. Others waited for ten days in the meadow in tents, without water and under extremely difficult conditions. You call that a tourist resort? That was a camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, I would spend up to a month on voluntary work drives in tents, and I never considered myself being a camp. And you were in tents in Palic next to the lake of Palic, and what are you saying? The people who had money, they got a passport in two days and those who didn't got it in ten days?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you forget that those hosts of ours, as you call them, and they were our guards, were men under arms, very dirty, people who kept talking about fighting in Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I assume they did lecture you about fighting in Croatia and Bosnia, but somehow it doesn't seem to fit that people came to help you from the Suboticanka factory, they gave you fruit juices, they drank with you, you have photographs taken with them next to the train, a refugee train, travelling. They don't even treat you as refugees because you were still citizens of an existing state of Yugoslavia, so they helped you to get passports in the closest Secretariat of Internal Affairs, that is in Subotica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question? He's told you that they received passports. He's given his evidence about it. Now, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't that assistance? Was your intention to go to Western Europe?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be assistance if we were not in the camp, if we did not have to pay dearly for those passports. It would be assistance if we were not mistreated. Those who had a large sum of money got passports. Those of us who didn't have money, waited for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you have to wait for it, those of you who didn't have money?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five, six, seven, eight days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let the citizens of Yugoslavia hear you that you had to wait all of five, six, seven or eight days to get a passport. And then all those with passports, let them remind themselves how many of them had to wait for five, six, seven, or eight days to get a passport, for the formalities to be completed when one normally applies for a passport, for a passport to be printed, registered, and handed over to the recipient.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Waiting in one's own apartment in one's own town is one thing, and waiting in a meadow in a tent without food or water, with war cries is something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that there were some Indians surrounding you, shouting war cries.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were your Chetniks waging war in Croatia and Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, I had no Chetniks of my own. As you know full well, Mr. Banjanovic, but I see that you have every intention of giving that impression. But never mind. Let's go on. Let's go back now to your Kozluk, which, as you say, is a well-known town. I really do regret that I had never heard of it. You say -- tell me, please, on that day, the 26th of May [as interpreted], how many soldiers were there in your Kozluk, of all possible types, troops, paramilitary, police, everything?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was about 1.000 to 1.300 households. In front of each there was two to three soldiers. So there were more than 3.000 members of the army, paramilitary units, police force, Territorial Defence units. I had never seen so many men of that kind, because Kozluk was surrounded by Serbian villages. So there were more than 3.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Banjanovic. As you were president of the local commune there and you were familiar with what was going on there, tell me, please, how can you explain the purpose for which those 3.000 men under arms had come to Kozluk? Were 3.000 of them needed to force you to move out or do anything else?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For several days Radio Loznica, which is in Serbia, and Radio Zvornik, which is in Zvornik in Bosnia, exerted media pressure, claiming that we had guns, weapons, that we were well-armed. Then an APC of the Yugoslav People's Army with the words "The Drina Corps" inscribed on it was roaming around Kozluk and the surrounding places, calling on the people to surrender the weapons and to surrender the people we were hiding. So there was a very strong media campaign on the radio and through loudspeakers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, there were no Yugoslav People's Army troops there but there was only the Territorial Defence or the army of Republika Srpska. There was no JNA forces there in Kozluk. Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Milosevic introduced himself in Kozluk to us as being the commander of the Drina Corps. He stated this at meetings. He told this to international people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this, please?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May, June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So not during these events.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on the 26th but before the 26th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there JNA members involved in these events?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was there from among the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people in uniform. For us, they were the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That is sufficient. Tell me, was anyone killed on the 26th of June in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days before that, Medo Marhocevic was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute, please. That was a few days before that. I can't enter into each individual incident. Just tell me, on the 26th, the day we're talking about when you were allegedly forced to leave Kozluk, was anyone killed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Galib Hadzic was seriously injured in the centre of Kozluk. A soldier shot at him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. He was wounded. But was anyone killed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You describe here that from all sides you were surrounded and that you were beaten and shot at. That was the description you gave.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were surrounded. We were herded into the centre of Kozluk. There was shooting on all sides to intimidate us, and houses were torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have taken note - and this can certainly be found in the transcript and on the tape it can be found as we are speaking the same language - you said they were shooting at the people. That is what you said, they shot at the people.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yet you say that no one was killed.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Galib Hadzic was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. There were 3.000 soldiers shooting at the people and this Galib Hadzic, one, is wounded?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were shooting into the air, they were shooting at the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, into the air. I see. And torching houses. I see. Then you say that your original documents were seized by members of the TO of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the military police, known as Studeni. He was head of the deportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not interested nor do I know him nor do I know your president of the municipality. So you're talking about the TO of Zvornik. Are you talking about Zvornik in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that these people that were rounding you up were listing you down together with the citizens of Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if they were forcing you out, why did the citizens of Kozluk make lists? Why was that necessary at all?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a commission in front of the cultural centre, and people signed their names on this list. And once they had done that, they were shoved into the buses and trucks without any luggage and without any food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can't believe that they left without luggage or food. And you say they were shoved into trucks and buses and trailers. And in this document, it says: "We examined the statements of 1.822 persons who were transported in 18 buses, three trucks, and two passenger vehicles from Kozluk." So most of the people were boarded onto buses; isn't that right? Seventeen buses, three trucks, and two passenger vehicles. That is what is said in this document. Is that incorrect?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, those buses and trucks arrived immediately we told we had to leave, which means that they had been prepared and organised. Secondly, there is room in one bus for 50 people. And you see how many there were. The buses and trucks were packed full. People were choking inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going to adjourn now. It's half past. Mr. Milosevic, we have in mind that this was a 92 bis witness, a Rule 92 bis witness, and therefore, you should have rather longer, but the time you can have is an hour and a half, which means you've got, if you want it, another three-quarters of an hour with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three-quarters of an hour, Mr. May, is not long enough, I think, because by putting this witness on the 92 bis, you have limited my cross-examination quite considerably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. And it would certainly be long enough if you didn't spend so long arguing with the witness. You've got three-quarters of an hour. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, in your statement it says that Kozluk had about 12.000 inhabitants. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. About 5.000 inhabitants. But with Sepak, Skocic, the surrounding places, it has about 12.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that information refers to the entire local commune, not just the village?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozluk is a local commune with about 5.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tell me, given that in this list of yours you had 1.822 people who went to Western Europe, that's what it says here, what happened to the other 3.200 inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the other citizens went to Western countries.
