utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So others went too.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Serbs lived in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were between 15 and 20 families there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many lived -- how many Serbs live there now?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 5.000 Serbs when we left Kozluk, and at the moment there are about 1.000 Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the second page of your statement you say that after the fall of Zvornik, Kozluk remained surrounded by the Serbian forces. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long these battles, this fighting in Zvornik lasted for?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many victims there were in that fighting?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how is it that, as you claim, Zvornik fell but Kozluk didn't? What was the difference?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Kozluk, the inhabitants of both nationalities remained loyal. There was no fighting in the centre itself. We lived in peace with our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were no attacks directed against Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not until the 20th, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the fighting in Zvornik, did you decide to form some sort of a Crisis Staff in your place; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs in that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs formed their own police forces and their Crisis Staff. So a number of citizens, inhabitants formed a Crisis Staff, and we would always meet together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you provided a list here. There were nine of you in the Crisis Staff, and that was before any kind of fighting broke out. So why, when you say that you lived on good terms with the Serbs in that place, why didn't you have a joint Crisis Staff, that you made a Crisis Staff -- you formed a Crisis Staff for Muslims alone?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Serbs separated themselves. They separated the police. In time, they formed their own units, their own staff, et cetera. They didn't want to be together with the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Serbs didn't want this but you did?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was there a defence plan, a plan to defend the place, that you discussed at the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your personal duties in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our task was to establish contact with neighbouring places in which people of Serbian nationality lived, with Tabanci, Malesici, Rici, Skocic, and other places, in order to attempt -- in order to avoid a war, because we had always lived on good terms until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this is why I'm asking you why you needed this war, since the terms you were on with others were good. Tell me, was there any contact with Muslim paramilitary formations, you as a crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you say you engaged two Muslims and sent them on some sort of spy mission among the Serb forces to see what was going on there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what you claim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the sixth paragraph -- I've only received your statement in English although I believe that you didn't give your statement into English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it says here: [In English] "I asked two Muslims, one of them was a forester, to inquire what was going on all surrounding areas for our security. They saw military training performed by those people in the vicinity of Kozluk. They told what they had seen --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness find it. Have you found that, Mr. Banjanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just make sure you have it in front of you. Yes, go on reading. It's page 2, sixth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these aren't my words, they're your words. So please tell me, what were the names of these two Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was called Nijaz Marhosevic, and the other person, and the other person was called Redjo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their duty? Were they obliged to follow your orders?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was not an order of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this mission a dangerous one for them?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what a forester does in forests. It's his job to be in forests. You know what the duty of a guard consist of. He had to be present in the forest. We didn't send the fire brigade there, we sent people whose work this was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You sent them to see what was happening. As you say in your statement, you approached the Serbian soldiers and you openly asked them what they were doing there, and they answered to you in a friendly way that Grujic had called them there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tell me, how is it that your place was surrounded since you were free to move around, to move through enemy ranks and talk about the reasons for their presence there, et cetera? How can you talk about there being an encirclement?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Serbian forces had encircled Kozluk from all sides. And also encircled by the Territorial Defence, paramilitary units, and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you say there were Serbian villages around you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, even 20 years ago it was encircled by Serbs; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there were no trenches at the time and there were no armed soldiers at the time, and at the time, one year back, there weren't various exercises, training manoeuvres, firing, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did those two men of yours see, the two men that you sent on a mission?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't go to reconnoiter. They carried out their usual duties as foresters. They saw a certain number of unknown people who had bands on which it said Military Scouts. They saw that these people were armed, and they also saw that these people were training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they observed them carrying out military exercises without hindrance.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was from a great distance, through binoculars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were covered -- they were under cover?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I see, they informed someone called Redjo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Redjo is a policeman. He is from the local police in Zvornik, and he was a worker in -- he works as a policeman in Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why they informed him, because he was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then as I can -- as I see in your statement, he -- that is to say, Redjo went straight to Zvornik. He went to the police station.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to hand over all the proof of these activities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So according to what comes out of what you have just confirmed, Zvornik fell, the Serbs laid siege to Kozluk, and Redjo went to Zvornik that had allegedly been taken and told the Serbs that the Serbs were training.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are distorting what I said. You're distorting the facts. This happened before the fall of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even earlier on?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well then. In the eighth paragraph on the same page, you say that the Serbs from Ugljari, Malesici, and Tabanci built a big road although there was a good road that passed through Kozluk; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tell me, why didn't you mention this?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because at the time, heavy military machines appeared in Serbian villages alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were building a road and this is something that was suspicious; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why would it be suspicious to build roads?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there were two roads already in existence. That's a little too much. It was a matter of connecting the Serbian villages in the Serbian territory in order to bypass Kozluk. You've asked me this on two occasions. Is it necessary to ask me a third time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement, you say that the Serbian policemen, almost all the arms and vehicles from the police station in Zvornik was transported to Celopek; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that that happened?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when I went there to the Crisis Staff on several occasions with a special permit, I saw that there was a large number of police vehicles, and I saw that there were a lot of police present there, et cetera. And Radio Zvornik said that this Ministry of the Interior, this police station, had been divided into a Muslim and Serbian part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that basis you concluded that they had transported weapons to Celopek?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I went to the Crisis Staff and to Zvornik, when I was provided with a special permit, I saw that there were many vehicles there and many policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you came to that conclusion on that basis?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You say that the Serbian paramilitary formations attacking Safka [phoen] and Kovacevic [phoen], these villages, they passed through your place very often and they were afraid of the inhabitants' reaction, but fortunately, nothing happened; isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tell me, how is it that the Serbian forces attacked all the surrounding places and even passed through your place in order to attack others but they kept bypassing Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They passed through Kozluk. In Kozluk there was the Serbian and the Bosniak police, and they had joint patrols. There were two Crisis Staffs in Kozluk and they cooperated. There was contact with the neighbouring places, and there was mutual respect in Kozluk, because we had always lived in peace. There were no incidents in Kozluk. It's true that those paramilitary units and the army came and passed through, but they didn't disturb us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When you say in the surrounding places, you are referring to the Serbian places, the Serbian villages. Why had barricades been erected there?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why, but I know that a long time before that, a year before the conflict broke out, there was training of some kind, there were meetings, there were military scouts who had bands on them. These people were often seen. There was something happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know what.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is it true that your neighbours, your Serbian neighbours visited you and tried to convince you that nothing bad would happen to the Muslims and that there was no reason to be afraid?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Brano Grujic tell you about that at a meeting that was held with you at Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the mayor Grujic, we had several meetings at which Marko Pavlovic and others were present. At those meetings, he promised us that no one would touch us, that we could continue living in peace. He said that we should surrender those weapons and carry on working in the fields and not think about the frontline, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the only request that concerned military matters had to do with surrendering weapons?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4 of your statement, you say that the Muslim inhabitants from the village of Sepak and the village of Skocic who had left their places, you tried to persuade them to return to their village; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you too thought they weren't in any kind of danger from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a large number of Kozluk had appeared in Kozluk. There were about 12.000 people in Kozluk, and we no longer had any food. Illness -- illnesses were present. There was a lot of people from all the surrounding Bosniak villages in Kozluk, and it was an intolerable situation. So we then agreed that those people would return to their homes and no one would touch them. We said that everything would carry on in a peaceful manner, that there wouldn't be any attacks et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it true that the inhabitants from these villages were only requested to hand over heavy weapons which they didn't need, not by any means unless they were preparing some sort of military action? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the most difficult thing was the fact that there was -- the media was constantly requesting that these guns and heavy weapons should be surrendered, but the Bosniaks really didn't possess any such weapons, the Bosniaks from Sepak and Kozluk, the surrounding places. Because we cooperated well with the Serbs and with Serbia, we didn't have any weapons of any kind, and this was really evident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the inhabitants from Sepak and Skocic, were any of them killed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some men didn't want to go with us. They went to the free territory. They crossed over to the free territory and that is when they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the territory that was under the control of the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And that's where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed on the way there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you had tried to convince them, did the inhabitants from Sepak and Skocic return to their places?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vasilije Kacavenda was on a peace mission. There was Muhamed Lugavic, there was Marko Pavlovic, Brano Grujic, and myself. After a number of meetings, about 5.000 to 6.000 people returned to their houses in Sepak, Skocic and other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true to say that you contacted the JNA to help you if your place was attacked, if your village was attacked?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had faith in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right up to the time that I saw those military vehicles returning and when I realised that was no longer the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know that the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia was in order to satisfy the request of Alija Izetbegovic and his men?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that I saw large columns of tanks. There were military columns. I saw the JNA flag, but those people in those vehicles and those lorries, they weren't soldiers. They were terrible people. They were dirty. They were wearing various kinds of uniforms. They opened fire at my place. They gathered in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's not waste time on this, on the subject of firing in your place which didn't result in any casualties, there is no point in discussing this. But please tell us, you tell -- you're saying that in your office - and this is something you mentioned a minute ago, this is in Kozluk, it's on page 5 - you were met by Brano Grujic, Dragan Spasojevic, and Dr. Muhamed and Jokic, who was a Muslim; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then these three together, together with the hodza, Muhamed Efendija Lugavic and the Serbian priest Vasilije Kacavenda went to see the locals of Sepak and Skocic and appealed to them not to resort to force and not to attack the Serb barricades. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say then, please?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's written in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. How do you interpret this event when a Serbian-cum-Muslim delegation comprising men of religion were endeavouring to calm down the situation? Was that their main purpose?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This delegation's aim was to encourage the Bosniak population to return to their homes in the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is -- does this act indicate any intention on the part of the Serbs to attack these places or, on the contrary, to calm the situation down?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This delegation said that it could not take any responsibility, that there were higher placed people in Zvornik, higher-level commanders who could guarantee security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if on that occasion Grujic and Spasojevic addressed the people and said that no one would be hurt or arrested, that there was no cause for fear, that everyone should return to their homes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was their intention to intimidate and expel the Muslims from this area? Wouldn't they have said quite the opposite if that had been their aim?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened long before the deportation. Their aim was to break up this group of people because it was dangerous to have 12.000 Muslims in one place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But then you asked Grujic to see his superior.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He as the mayor said that he could not assume any responsibility and that there was someone higher up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you went to Karakaj, which is a part of Zvornik; isn't Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 20681 to 20691. it?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Grujic too wanted you to make sure you were safe?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Celopek you meant someone called Pejic?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see, in Karakaj. I'm sorry. In Karakaj. And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw that he really was the boss. A part of the delegation didn't even dare enter the office, whereas the others stood at attention in front of him. He received only the hodza Lugavic, the priest Kacavenda, and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said to Brano Grujic that we must be protected and that he should rule if he can. If not, he would be replaced. I asked that he personally should come and visit Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he insisted that you must be protected. And he said to Grujic that he must perform his duty and take care of the citizens; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he didn't intimidate you, but on the contrary, indicated that he wanted to protect you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked us to surrender heavy weapons if we had any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That's only logical.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he could go to Kozluk and see for himself that we had nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that he gave you assurances that you should stay in your homes, that there was nothing to fear, and that all he requested was the surrender of heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you invited him to Kozluk. He accepted the invitation. And then you set off to Kozluk immediately together; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that he addressed the people in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Offering the same guarantees he had given you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that he promised to provide food, medicines as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was appalled by the difficult situation he witnessed, and he saw a large number of children and sick people, and he sent some medicines and doctors and a truck full of food. What he promised to 10 to 12.000 people, he kept. He kept his promise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Pejic say to you that if you wanted to leave nevertheless, that it was very dangerous for you to head towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He told us that we could never pass along that route to Tuzla. He said, "If you go to Tuzla, you will join the army and you will wage war against us." That is what he said. And I saw a very, very large number of barricades and lots of men under arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a frontline there somewhere?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The frontline was removed from Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, a distance away, but in the direction of Tuzla, and that is why you couldn't go towards Tuzla, because it was unsafe for you.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he told you that you could go in the direction of Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while, we were totally surrounded and in total isolation, and the only exit led towards Serbia. And also, we had to have special passes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you all left to Serbia without any special passes, only having signed this list of people who wanted to go to Western Europe.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the people who left before. About 3.000 people had left before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to those people?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people who remained in Kozluk, who didn't want to leave with us, were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were killed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More than 20 men were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were these people killed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 26th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you had left already.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who killed them?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those same guards, those same men that had surrounded Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I can see from your statement, Pejic released several people from Kozluk, trusting your statement that they were not members of the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I see from your statement, you don't know the names of those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There was a neighbour called Idriz. His sister got married to somebody from Skocic and left there and then he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew all of them that you guaranteed about?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Serb policeman told me about them, and I went and made the request, and they were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were released because you guaranteed that they were not members of the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were ordinary citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you distinguish members of the Green Berets from others?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no Green Berets in my areas. I don't even know who those Green Berets were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And you say that from the 20th to the 25th of June, shooting could be heard in the environs of Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any fighting going on there, combat operations?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kozluk, it was quite peaceful, and people still believed in co-existence. Immediately prior to the deportation, Marko Pavlovic and other paramilitary units started their reign of terror in the surrounding villages. They mistreated Serbs. They made them strip. They beat them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reason was that they were too close to us Bosniaks. A large number of people were beaten up. A large number of people were mistreated by these paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So paramilitary units are -- were mistreating Serbs because they were on friendly terms with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, as I have a piece of information here, I want to check whether it is correct. It has to do with this fact that at one point, that is on the 26th of June, they told you that they could no longer guarantee your security; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the order issued to me by Brano Grujic that we should immediately leave Kozluk, a member of parliament called Mijatovic came up to me and said that there was no safety any more and that it would be best for us to leave because there could be a massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what was the reason for this?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason was, but I did see that in Zvornik and around it no one had control any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the chaos of a civil war.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There was a conflict among the Serbs themselves, among various paramilitary units, units of the army and so on. Nobody knew who was in command any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's exactly what I'm saying. A chaotic situation typical of a civil war. Do you know a village called Rastosnica? How far it from Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite far, I see. Has this anything to do with the fact that it was right then that the Muslim forces had destroyed that village and expelled more than 4.000 people from the area, Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were totally isolated and we didn't know what was happening a kilometre away from us not to mention 50 or 100 kilometres away. We just saw these various armies passing through Kozluk. Something was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So several thousand people from this destroyed village fled to your area, according to my information.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, no one arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true that in Kozluk nothing was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could it be destroyed when there was no war there? Maybe 50 up to 100 houses were destroyed that were already old, and a number of houses were damaged or torched during the deportation. But the number is very small.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as opposed to Rastosnica which was totally destroyed and 4.000 people expelled from it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness knows nothing about that. There's no point repeating it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But the witness does know that Kozluk was not destroyed, that there was no war there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've had the evidence about that. He's given it at some length.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Red Cross received you in Serbia - we discussed this at the very beginning - in view of the circumstances that we have just addressed, you yourself say there was chaos, conflict, even conflicts between various Serb formations, between Serb formations and Muslim formations. It doesn't matter which. You don't know of any Green Berets or the Patriotic League or anything like that. You say the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Anyway, you were evacuated. You arrived in Serbia. Did the Serbs save your life perhaps in doing this? Because you are talking of the circumstances under which you left. They told you they could no longer guarantee your safety, and you yourself described the situation as chaotic. By helping you to evacuate, did they save your life?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they lied to us. We were tricked. We didn't go to war. We surrendered our weapons. Why were we expelled from our jobs? Why didn't they let us till our land?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's another question. You yourself described a moment ago the chaotic situation, the shooting and everything else, and that you were told that they could no longer guarantee your safety. So my question is: By helping you evacuate, did they save your lives?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wrote this letter saying that we were doing everything voluntarily, but in fact, they expelled us. We left in trucks, in buses. The stoning, the beating, the killings was not an act of benevolence but an act of expulsion. Why would 5.000 people leave their homes? That is ethnic cleansing. That was the scenario.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Out of fear of war. Why do refugees all over the world leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not at war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've exhausted this topic. Move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did everyone have to leave Kozluk or only the people who wanted to?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about the departure and whether it was under force. Did everyone have to leave Kozluk or only the people who wanted to leave and who wanted to go to the West?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a voluntary matter. It was an order that we should leave immediately. It was ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us leave the qualification of this to someone else. Tell me, how many people stayed behind in Kozluk? If 1.822 of you signed that paper, how many stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb families and some Bosniaks who didn't want to go with us. And all those Bosniaks were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So those 20 Bosniaks only stayed behind. You said that 20 were killed and now you say all of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you a precise answer. The Bosniaks who didn't want to go with us were killed. There were some 20 of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So let's make sure we have this right. There were a number of Serbs, and you say 20 Bosniaks who stayed behind; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many Serbs there were? Can you give us some idea of that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said 15 households. There were 15 Serbian households.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were between 15 and 20 Serbian families. Those Serbs remained in Kozluk. Nobody disturbed them. They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I gathered that nobody disturbed you either. They suggested that you leave because they could no longer guarantee your safety because of what was going on in your environs.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't want to hear me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do want to hear you.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army, para-army and the police were herding people into the centre. They were opening fire. Medo Marhocevic was killed. Hadzic was wounded. Several houses were torched. Quite a lot of people were slapped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Medo was not killed on that day.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd, 24th he was killed but certainly not during that particular event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, you said a moment ago that on that day, no one was killed except for that one person being wounded. Very well. Now, tell me, how did the Serbs carry out ethnic cleansing by expelling Bosniaks to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter entirely for the Trial Chamber in due course, to characterise it and decide what happened. You've heard -- all he can do is give his evidence. He said they were sent to Serbia. Any qualification, as he rightly said, as you rightly said, is a matter for others, in fact for the Trial Chamber. Let's move on. You've got about, I should think, about five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll try, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put this question to him because, Mr. Banjanovic, I thought you were the head of the Association for the Return of Citizens of Bosniak Nationality of the Municipality of Zvornik; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm the president of the association for the return of all people to their territory, and that includes Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true to say that the government of the Federation of BH exerted pressure on the Muslims from Podrinje in order to get them to leave Podrinje and to move to the Sarajevo municipalities?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your association on the 23rd of May, 1996 - and I'm speaking about your association - did they issue a communique in which they condemned the government for such demographic policies?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were against any form of transporting, transferring people. We wanted people to return to their homes, and we wanted trust among citizens to be re-established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But since I'm asking you whether they exerted pressure, did the government exert pressure to make Bosniaks from Podrinje, to make Muslims move out? You say that you're not aware of that, but your association condemned the government for the exertion of such pressure. Are you aware of this fact or not?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We condemned all institutions that encouraged people to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell me, explain to me, what did the BH federation government want to achieve by exerting such pressure and by encouraging the people to move out?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not the Prime Minister, I'm just an ordinary citizen of Kozluk, and I want to live in Kozluk and to live on good terms with everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But you are aware of the fact that the government exerted pressure on the Podrinje Muslims so that they would move out from that territory. You're not aware of that fact, nor are you aware of any form of pressure exerted by the Muslims and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said that. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since I no longer have -- since I have no more time, I only have one more question for you, and this concerns the beginning of my cross-examination, what you said at the end when you -- concerning your arrival in Serbia, according to what you said. In Loznica, you asked the Red Cross for help. You asked them to help you continue your journey to Western Europe. Did they, as this is what you requested from them, could they have assumed, could they have known that you were deported or did they consider you to be refugees?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we were forced out of Kozluk. We were expelled from Kozluk. Twenty Bosniaks were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just answer this, Mr. Banjanovic: Can you say from your knowledge whether the Red Cross knew what your position was, that you were deported or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they did know. As soon as they saw us in the lorries, they knew that we were being deported. And we also told them what we had been through. We told them about what had happened. People were aware of the fact that this was a matter of deportation, forced expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now claiming that you informed the Red Cross in Loznica of the fact that you weren't refugees but that you were being forcibly deported by the authorities from the municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it that this does not appear on any of the documents that have been provided?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to ask those who compiled these documents. We didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you only contacted the Red Cross apart from the police that protected you. So you informed the Red Cross that you weren't leaving of your own free will and that the list that you had signed was a list that had been compiled under duress and that nothing -- none of this was correct. So why did you ask them to help you leave for Western Europe as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what you are claiming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But -- I'm sorry. But you said, and it's in the transcript, we asked them to help us continue our journey to Western Europe or, rather, you did not want to stay on in Loznica, you wanted to carry on. That's what you stated today.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received an order from Mr. Marko Pavlovic in Kozluk according to which we were leaving on a voluntary basis and that we were trying to avoid the mobilisation. But this is something he wrote down. We didn't. It's a lie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, I'm asking you to explain to me your testimony that you gave here this morning according to which you asked the Red Cross in Loznica to enable you to carry on your trip to Western Europe as soon as possible. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you made such a request, if you asked them to help you go to Western Europe as soon as possible, how can you at the same time claim that you told them that you had been taken there by force and that in fact you didn't want to carry on?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what you are saying. I said that we had been taken there, I said that we were hostages and that we wanted to go as far away from Serbia as possible, and I asked them to help us, and they said that they would send a document to Belgrade. I don't know what they wrote in that document, but they wrote it, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They didn't write anything. They sent your list, because in that document from Belgrade, it states, and I'll remind you of this, it states quite clearly here: "We have examined the written statements, the 1.822 people in 17 buses, three trucks with trailers, and two passenger vehicles from Kozluk, Zvornik municipality, and they now have permission. The written statements of the above-mentioned persons, given on their own behalf, on behalf of their under aged family members or children, et cetera, expressed their will as to where they want to live, which is one of the fundamental human rights. So they examined your list, the list that you had written and signed. They forwarded it to Belgrade and they requested that they should enable you to carry on. They replied that they had examined the list, decided that it was a matter of human rights that had to be respected, and they provided you with authorisation, with permission to carry on.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have failed to read is that the commander of the Territorial Defence in Zvornik, Marko Pavlovic, wrote down that we were leaving on a voluntary basis, that we were trying to avoid mobilisation and that we were putting our property down on a voluntary basis, that we were doing everything on a voluntary basis, that we hadn't been beaten, that none of our property has been torched, that we weren't being transported, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we have been over this several times, and we're not going to go over it again. We have the documents. We've heard the evidence. Now, Mr. Milosevic, your time is now up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that document, and you claim that the facts mentioned in it are false, you had that in your hands and it contains your handwriting.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why didn't you draw the attention of any of the Serbian authorities to the fact that it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed the Red Cross in Loznica, and I informed Mr. Nikolic of this fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Banjanovic, I think there is a matter that hasn't been fully clarified. As far as I have understood you, perhaps you could repeat this, you said that in your local commune there were 12.000 people in total.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say then?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 5.000 people in Kozluk. And in Skocic, Sepak, the surrounding places, together with Kozluk there were about 12.000 Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's concentrate on Kozluk which had 5.000 inhabitants. Given what you have just explained to the Trial Chamber now, if only 1.822 people left Kozluk and followed the route that you indicated, does that mean that a little over 3.000 people remained in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were about 5.000 inhabitants in Kozluk, and from the beginning of the conflict until the time of the deportation on the 26th, about 3.000 people left and went to foreign countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which routes did they follow to go to these foreign countries?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some crossed over into Serbia. For a certain period of time it was possible to go to Tuzla until that total blockade, when we were subjected to a total blockade. Then it was only possible to go to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those people who had previously passed through Serbia, did they leave on a voluntary basis or in some other manner?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They received permits and they left on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these people who followed other routes, through Tuzla, et cetera, did they also leave on a voluntary basis?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only these 1.822 people didn't leave on a voluntary basis?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I have understood you, in addition to this joint declaration, there were individual declarations given by each one of you according to which you wanted to leave and go to a foreign country.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was just this joint statement?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a list that we signed, and there was an order from the Territorial Defence which had been brought in an envelope. We didn't sign any kind of a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber whether all of these 1.822 people left Serbia and carried on?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that the 1.822 people, all of them had valid passports?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They had all been provided with valid passports.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps about a hundred people had passports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the others got it in Subotica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long it takes for such a procedure in order to issue passports and do you know that each passport has to be paid for, certain fees have to be paid?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were joint passports, and it had been paid by the Suboticanka factory. They paid very well for this. They brought six photographs -- photographers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now explain to the Trial Chamber the following: The Serbian Red Cross escorted you through the territory in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were escorted by the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Red Cross representatives?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who met you when you crossed the Yugoslav border? Was a sort of reception organised for you?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was the last one to get off. There were trains that took us there, to the stations, and we were sent further on then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those representatives of -- were these foreign representatives of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they had plans for where you should continue to?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they had any plans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were sent to specific places?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were sent to camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were then sent further on to Europe.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To join up with our families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have a question before Mr. Groome re-examines the witness. Questioned by the Court

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, you said that you were not allowed to leave the column while you were in Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does that mean there were some refugees who wished to remain in Serbia but were not allowed to do so and forced to move on to going --

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How many of them?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, not a very large number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell the story to me in detail about the refugees who wished to remain in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a lot of people worked in Serbia. There were quite a few mixed marriages. When we were expelled, we were in a column in Loznica, so leaving the vehicles was not permitted. We weren't permitted to leave the vehicles, and we dared not do so because there were a lot of armed people, armed men moving around the convoy, moving around the column. They asked for money, and they were looking for girls. They wanted the girls to get out of the vehicles. The people were afraid to leave the trailers, the lorries, the buses. The police who were present there didn't allow anyone to leave these vehicles. After an hour or two, a large number of policemen arrived, four to five police cars. There were a lot of policemen who didn't allow us to leave the buses and the lorries, to get off the buses and lorries. While we were carrying on, we had very little time. When we were getting onto the train we had to do so very quickly because they were stoning us from all directions. They stoned us. What else could the people do other than run into the trains, run into the carriages? They stoned the train on several occasions. When we arrived in Subotica, we were hungry. We were tired. A lot of people had been beaten, had injuries to their heads. It was a difficult trip. And I'll repeat this: While we were being deported from Kozluk, none of the citizens was allowed to take anything, neither food nor footwear nor clothes. Several families had relatives in Sepak and in other towns they had relatives too and they wanted to go and visit them. The police didn't allow them to do so. They didn't allow anyone to leave the convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm interested in those refugees who wished to remain in the territory of Serbia. Were they not able to talk to the Red Cross people, when they had a chance to talk with them, about their wish to remain in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the only person who spoke to the Red Cross, and I told them about this wish, but the people from the Red Cross said it would be better for them to go because of the war, because of the extremely difficult situation, because of the tension. And at that point, we all decided to leave in that column. We all decided that no one should remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, I want to ask you a couple of additional questions regarding Prosecution Exhibit 445, tab 7. I ask that be handed to the witness. And that is the document issued by the Republic of Serbia Commission for Refugees. My first question to you is: How much time elapsed between the time the Red Cross representative left you saying that they were going to seek authorisation for the convoy to continue and the time that that representative returned with tab 7 of Prosecution Exhibit 445?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything moved on very quickly. About two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we were to accept the contents of tab 7 on face value, in that two hours, the information you provided the Red Cross would have had to have been sent up to Belgrade. The first line of the document says: "We looked into the written statements of 1.822 persons." That would have had to have been done. Tab 7 would have had to have been drafted, and it would have had to have been sent down to Loznica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The copy that you saw, that you were presented with in Loznica, was it a fax copy or was it an original?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a fax.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the last line of the first paragraph, and there's an assertion there that you and the other people from Kozluk were temporarily residing in Loznica. During the course of your trip from Kozluk and out of Serbia, did you spend even one night in Loznica?

utterances.speaker: FADIL BANJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't stay in Loznica. We were in lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Banjanovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: May I raise an administration point with respect to the last witness. I neglected to refer on the record to the portion of the videotape that was played. That was an excerpt from Prosecution Exhibit 342, tab 13. The time -- the time of that excerpt was 22 minutes and 47 seconds to 24 minutes and 19 seconds. Your Honour Judge May, in a ruling of the 16th of October of last year, you made a ruling that we would deal with that particular exhibit excerpt by excerpt. We will work with the registrar later today to identify all the references to that exhibit and perhaps then a unique tab number or exhibit number can be assigned to the exhibit or this portion of that exhibit which was displayed here in court with this past witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That sounds sensible. Yes, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. de la Brosse is the next witness, the expert. Your Honour, there is a large number of exhibits with this witness. May they be given a collective exhibit number with tab numbers dealing with individual exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Prosecution Exhibit 446.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I intend to take a little time, but not very much, with the witness going through his report so that its structure can be understood by those viewing the proceedings and the Chamber may be reminded of the structure and along the way to deal with a few sample paper exhibits and a few - I can't remember how many - about ten or so, video clips. It may be convenient, if the Chamber's sorting its papers, if it finds the curriculum vitae of the witness, which I certainly shan't be taking in detail, and also the index to his report. The index is not at the moment numbered by pages. I'd ask that a copy of it go on the overhead projector if we can find a spare copy of the index itself which is at pages 2 and 3 of the report, but I'll be able to take you to the relevant pages quite easily. When we look at paper exhibits, I'm afraid I will not be selecting them from sequential tab numbers. I hope that won't be inconvenient. I will be able to identify the tab numbers and have the relevant short extracts placed on the overhead projector so it may be in that way the Chamber won't be too inconvenienced. I certainly hope not. And, Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness to come in, with some regret that perhaps Mr. Lopez-Terres isn't here, bearing in mind his approach to these matters in an earlier case, I can tell you that the witness will be giving his evidence in French, and I think, if not the first, one of the first witnesses in the trial to give evidence in what is, after all, one of the two official languages of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: Renaud de la Brosse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your occupation, Mr. de la Brosse?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: I'm a professor at the University of Reims in the Champagne Ardennes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're here to give evidence about propaganda and you've provided an extensive curriculum vitae which is available to the Judges as an exhibit in this case and will thus be available in due course to others who seek it because it's publicly filed, but let's focus on the relevant part of your experience. Have you been in research work and otherwise concerned with the role of the press in political transition and crisis since about 1991?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I have been interested in the role of the media and their position in relation to political changes which took place in Eastern Europe and in Africa during the 1980s and the beginning of the 1990s. That is the subject of my doctoral thesis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the course of your research, have you not only considered traditional matters like Armenia and Nazi Germany but performed case studies on various occasions?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: Yes. In 1994 I was in charge of a work that was published at the publishing house Decouverte, which is a series of case studies - there were nine - and these retraced the negative role of the media in propagating images of hatred and racism. Those case studies took place in Africa. This was -- there was a case that I studied in Burundi and Rwanda and in Eastern Europe, using the case of the former Yugoslavia, which I wrote myself, and as part of a study on Romania. And other case studies in other continents, including the Middle East, Palestine, Egypt and the Caucasus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally, and that is not particularly focusing on propaganda, has your work been acceptable to UNESCO in studies on West African matters, and also to the European Community on other topics?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: I did in fact have the opportunity to carry out several studies for UNESCO and the European Commission. The last study that I did for the European Commission was in September of 2002, and it dealt with regulating communications in sub-Saharan Africa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you prepared reports from time to time for various NGOs and in particular for Reporters Sans Frontieres?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I did some missions for them in Africa in 1994 in Guinea, Conakry, and in Guinea-Bissau. In addition, I was involved in drafting a report for the French Ministry of Defence on the development of a meeting in Africa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the time you were commissioned by the Office of the Prosecutor to prepare a report on propaganda over an extended period of time in the former Yugoslavia, were you already in possession of some materials that related to the former Yugoslavia as a result of your earlier case study?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I began to work on Yugoslavia specifically in 1994 when I was directing the work and working directly with the case study on the former Yugoslavia. In addition, I continued to work on that, going into more depth in an article that was published in a collective study led by General Cot in 1997, and I also worked on propaganda in an article which I published further to the war in Kosovo dealing with journalism. And I also was interested in propaganda through the media in Africa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then being commissioned to prepare this report by the Office of the Prosecutor, were you provided with further materials, substantially from newspapers but also videos?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And those materials, Your Honour, are identified in the exhibits and in particular in tab 2 of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to my own archives, I used some firsthand material. These were either written press articles or extracts of television programmes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you to Ms. Dicklich, it's really tab 3, not tab 2. Before we turn to the report itself, should we just observe this: The report was filed publicly in these proceedings as long ago as I think about February of this year. Have you received in respect of it any negative comment by those who may have claimed access to it and read it?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: I know that there was an article in a Berlin newspaper. I believe that it was positive, and I know that there was an article on an internet site. And in addition, I -- I know that the official from the Reuters office in Belgrade in 1991, apparently he was -- he challenged an article that was published in Politika. I don't have the date. I don't have the article with me here. He also challenged the fact that it was at the source of the distribution of information about 41 babies allegedly massacred by the Ustasha in Vukovar in November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard any more from that particular person since this first comment on your report?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from him, has there been any other negative comment by general readers or peers who may have read your report, it being available since February?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Propaganda, it may be accepted by you, is something used by all sides in all wars these days. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have focused in your report on the use by either the accused or the Serb interests of propaganda, but have you also given some consideration to the use made by the other protagonists in these conflicts, of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: You're speaking about Yugoslavia, are you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: Yes. In this article that I wrote in 1994, out of reasons of intellectual honesty, I thought I needed to use a comparative approach, using the documents I had available to me. That is, several articles, including NGO reports whose objective was to defend press freedom in the media, I got some information from there. They were either reports or press releases or warnings that had been sent to various chiefs of government at the time. I said -- I wrote that that propaganda was used by each of the republics at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report you express a view as to the comparative use of propaganda by the different sides. How would you support the view as to whether one side or another was using propaganda more extensively; from your earlier work or from some other way?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 67 of the report, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I base myself on what I had access to at the time that the article was being written and also on conversations which I had with journalists or intellectuals. By that I mean people from universities or other people who were interested in those issues and who confirmed to me that on the Serbian side propaganda had spread out over a much longer period of time than in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Croatia. And in addition, the intensity of that propaganda apparently seems to have been greater. In particular, through the written press, if we look at the daily Politika which, until it was taken over by the Serb nationalist elements at the end of 1991 was really an institution in Serbia. It was a newspaper which was given credit of being extremely professional, and the setting up of a column that was called -- we called in French co-reactions or -- led to the production of 4.000 articles in which the themes of Serbian resentment are developed in respect of the other communities. And that column went on for about three years, if I'm correct. I think it was -- I think it was from 1988 to 1991. And it was a sum of articles which were very important. And I did not find, if I'm not mistaken, I didn't find from -- at least from conversations I was able to have with other journalist colleagues, I didn't find such examples in Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia. Having said this, this observation is not actually based on an exhaustive comparative study.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we now place on the overhead projector, and leave it there, the index to your report first. It's in two pages. This will enable those viewing the proceedings to know the structure of the document that the learned Judges and the parties have had an opportunity to consider as we take a few samples from what you have written. Did you, as the index reveals -- go to the next page, please. Did you start off your report with a part headed Political Propaganda, Definitions, Fundamental Principles and Yugoslav Particularities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that runs between pages 4 and 9 of the report. And I think the only points that I would seek to emphasise at this stage can be found first of all in the report itself at page 4, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You set out here something of which the Special Rapporteur appointed by the United Nations was able to deal with in a report of 1994 where he explained in respect to the former Yugoslavia that, since the fighting began and information put out by the media of the former Yugoslavia has mainly consisted of national discourse and generalised attacks and insults aimed at other people, he was able to go on to make this point: "It comes as no surprise that the phenomenon has directly led to the perpetration of horrible atrocities on the fields of battle and throughout the entire territory." Now, that observation, does that underline in any way the distinctions that you seek to draw perhaps between propaganda that may be acceptable and propaganda that may not be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look then at tab 27, paragraph -- another report of the General Assembly, and I'll put on the overhead projector paragraph 206 of it. In another report dated 1995, we see this passage: "Nationalist rhetoric and sweeping attacks and slurs against other peoples have been a dominant feature of news propagated in the former Yugoslavia's media since the start of the conflicts. Not surprisingly, this phenomenon has led directly to the commission of fearful atrocities on the battlefields ..." Insofar as you can consider this, and you mustn't stray beyond your appropriate area of expertise, but insofar as you are able to consider this, does the material that you have seen and reviewed fit with that conclusion of the rapporteur and the report?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go then to the page 5 of the report. There are a couple of places where you draw on a book written by Borisav Jovic, of which the Chamber will be aware, and of course it will be for determination later whether the passage quoted is one upon which the Judges can rely. Nevertheless, for these purposes, we can see, and this can be found in its original or better form at tab 4, I quote here for the purposes of saving time, Borisav Jovic wrote this: "For years, he," speaking of the accused, "paid the biggest attention to the media, especially television. He personally appointed editors-in-chief of the newspapers and news programmes, especially directors-general of the radio and television. Perhaps in no other area but this was he in direct communication with all editors who 'fed' the public with the news, comments and generally with information. He was deeply convinced that citizens formed their view of the political situation on the basis of what they were presented and not on the basis of their real material and political position. What is not published has not happened at all - that was Milosevic's motto." How does that approach, if it be an accurate reflection of an approach, fit in with your understanding from other case studies of the use and effectiveness of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: RENAUD DE LA BROSSE
utterances.text: This statement of Borisav Jovic has been corroborated by other testimony of close -- people close to Mr. Milosevic. I think later on we'll have the occasion to review the excerpt of a review of Dusan Mitevic, who was the director of the RTS, in which he corroborates that first testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can I take you and the witness back to the UN report, paragraph 206 of which you've cited. I think that's tab 20 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Twenty-seven. The report makes the point with which the witness has agreed, that nationalistic rhetoric has led directly to the commission of fearful atrocities on the battlefield and throughout the territory. It's early in his testimony, but I would imagine that later on he will tell us how he is able to substantiate that connection, that link between nationalistic rhetoric and the commission of fearful atrocities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will deal with that later.
